title: A Clock on a Track
bigQuestion: How did a footrace on a dirt path become eight lanes, a measured lap and a time on paper?

story.title: A Hand Drops
story.kicker: At a spring meet, eight runners start at eight different marks and finish as eight written times.
paragraphs: It is a spring afternoon at an Illinois high school track. Eight runners wait in eight lanes. Their starting marks do not line up. The runner in lane eight stands far ahead of the runner in lane one.
The starter raises a hand, and the signal sounds. Near the finish line, a camera points straight across the track. A screen beside it waits to show each runner's time to the hundredth of a second.
One hundred years ago, this meet would have looked different. The track was likely made of crushed cinders. Timers stood at the line holding stopwatches. They wrote down times to a fifth of a second.

Nearly three thousand years ago, runners at Olympia in Greece raced on a straight dirt path. No one kept a clock at all. Judges simply named who crossed first. The oval, the lanes and the clock all came much later.
story.think: Why do you think the runners in the outside lanes start farther ahead?

lessons.title: A Straight Race at Olympia
lessons.mainIdea: The oldest known Olympic race was one length of a straight track called a stade.
reading: Olympia was a holy place in southern Greece. Greeks held games there to honor the god Zeus. By tradition, the first games took place in 776 BCE. Later Greek writers counted from that year.

The first race was one length of the *stadium*. That word comes from the Greek *stade*, a measure of length. At Olympia, the track was a straight strip of packed earth about 192 meters long. Runners raced from one end to the other.

The Greek writer Pausanias visited Olympia in the 100s CE. He wrote that the footrace was the only event at the first games. He named the winner as Coroebus of Elis. Historians treat these early lists as tradition, not as exact records.

words.d: a Greek measure of length, and the name of a one-length footrace
a place built for races; the word comes from stade
the holy place in Greece where the ancient Olympic Games were held

look.title: A Traveler at Olympia
look.text: Pausanias writes that at the first Olympic games there was only one contest, the footrace, and that Coroebus of Elis won it.
look.cite: Pausanias, Description of Greece, Book 5 (Elis I), 2nd century CE
look.prompt: Pausanias lived long after 776 BCE. How should that change how much we trust his list?

check.q: What was the stade?
choices: a Greek measure of length and a footrace
check.why: The stade was a Greek measure of length. The one-length footrace took its name.

check.q: What was the shape of the race path at Olympia?
choices: a straight strip of packed earth
check.why: Olympia's track was a straight earth strip about 192 meters long.

check.q: Who wrote that Coroebus won the first footrace?
check.why: Pausanias, a Greek travel writer, recorded that tradition.

lessons.title: Who Could Run at Olympia
lessons.mainIdea: Only free Greek men and boys could compete at the ancient Olympic Games.
reading: The ancient games had strict rules about who could enter. Athletes had to be free Greek men or boys. Enslaved people could not compete. People who were not Greek were also shut out.

Married women were not allowed to watch the men's games. Pausanias wrote that girls held their own footraces at Olympia. These were the Heraia, games honoring the goddess Hera. The girls ran a track shorter than the men's stade.
The modern Olympics began in Athens in 1896. Women did not run track events at the Olympics until 1928, in Amsterdam. That year, women raced the 100 meters and the 800 meters for the first time.

words.d: ancient footraces for girls at Olympia, honoring the goddess Hera
to keep someone out by a rule

look.title: Two Tracks at One Place
look.text: At Olympia, men's races honored Zeus on the long stade. Girls' races honored Hera on a shorter track. Married women could not even watch the men's games. More than 2,000 years later, women first ran Olympic track races in 1928.
look.prompt: What rules decided who could run at Olympia? How did those rules change over time?

check.q: Who could compete in the ancient men's Olympic games?
check.why: Only free Greek men and boys could enter the ancient games.

check.q: What were the Heraia?
check.why: Pausanias wrote about the Heraia, girls' races honoring Hera.

check.q: When did women first run track events at the modern Olympics?
check.why: Women first raced Olympic track events in Amsterdam in 1928.

lessons.title: Yards, Miles and Meters
lessons.mainIdea: Older American and British tracks used a 440-yard lap; the world later settled on 400 meters.
reading: In the 1800s, British and American runners measured races in yards and miles. Many tracks were one quarter of a mile around. That lap is 440 yards. Four laps made one *mile*.

France created the *meter* in the 1790s as a new measure. Most of Europe later used it for races. The modern Olympics measured track races in meters from 1896 on. A 440-yard lap is about 402 meters, a little longer than 400.

Two measures made trouble. A time for 440 yards could not sit on the same list as a time for 400 meters. Over the 1900s, most American high school and college tracks switched to meters. Today the outdoor lap is 400 meters in almost every country.

words.d: an English measure of distance equal to 1,760 yards
a measure of length made in France; the unit of the modern lap
one full trip around a track

look.title: Track Lengths in Meters
look.cite: World Athletics, Technical Rules (200 m indoor and 400 m outdoor tracks); U.S. customary units (440 yards = 402.3 m; 1 mile = 1,609.3 m)
look.prompt: How much longer is the old quarter-mile lap than the standard outdoor lap?

check.q: How long was a quarter-mile lap?
check.why: A quarter of a mile is 440 yards.

check.q: Why could a 440-yard time not share a list with a 400-meter time?
choices: The races were in different lanes.
The distances were not the same.
check.why: 440 yards is about 402 meters, so the races were different lengths.

check.q: Where was the meter first created?
check.why: France created the meter in the 1790s.

lessons.title: The World's Track Rules
lessons.mainIdea: A world body, now called World Athletics, writes the rules that make every standard track the same.
reading: In 1912, leaders from many countries met in Stockholm, Sweden. They formed the International Amateur Athletic Federation, or IAAF. Its job was to write one set of track rules. It also kept the list of official world records.

The IAAF renamed itself *World Athletics* in 2019. Its rule book says a standard outdoor track is 400 meters in the inside lane. Each *lane* may be up to 1.22 meters wide. Most standard tracks have eight lanes.

School tracks in the United States follow a rule book from the National Federation of State High School Associations, or NFHS. The IHSA uses NFHS rules for Illinois meets. Those rules also measure races in meters.

words.d: the world body that writes track rules; called the IAAF from 1912 to 2019
a marked strip of track that one runner stays in
the National Federation of State High School Associations, which writes U.S. high school rule books

look.title: The Standard Track
look.text: The rule book describes a standard track as 400 meters long in the inside lane, with lanes no wider than 1.22 meters.
look.cite: World Athletics, Competition and Technical Rules, rules on the running track
look.prompt: Why would every country want its tracks built to the same size?

check.q: What was World Athletics called before 2019?
check.why: It was the International Amateur Athletic Federation, formed in 1912.

check.q: Where was the world track body founded in 1912?
check.why: Leaders met in Stockholm, Sweden, in 1912.

check.q: Whose rule book do Illinois high school meets use?
check.why: The IHSA uses the NFHS rule book for its meets.

lessons.title: Why Starts Are Staggered
lessons.mainIdea: Staggered starting marks make every lane the same distance in a race that goes around a curve.
reading: A track has two straight sides and two curves. On a curve, an outer lane makes a bigger circle than an inner lane. If everyone started on one line, the outside runner would run farther.
So officials paint a *stagger*. That is a set of starting marks that step forward, lane by lane. The runner in lane eight starts farthest ahead. Each runner still covers exactly the same distance.
In races on one straight, like the 100 meters, everyone starts on the same line. Staggers matter only when the race runs around a curve. The finish line is one straight line across all lanes.

words.d: starting marks set farther forward in each outer lane so every lane is the same length
the bent end of a track, where outer lanes are longer

look.title: Circles Inside Circles
look.text: Picture two circles drawn on the ground, one inside the other. A small circle is shorter around than a big one. Now picture a track's eight lanes as eight curves, one inside the next. The starting marks step forward from lane one to lane eight.
look.prompt: Which lane would be longest if every runner started on one line?

check.q: What is a stagger?
choices: starting marks that step forward in outer lanes
check.why: A stagger moves the starting marks forward so every lane is equal.

check.q: Why is an outer lane longer around a curve?
choices: It is painted a different color.
check.why: Outer lanes make bigger circles, so they are longer.

check.q: Which race usually starts all runners on one line?
check.why: A race on one straight has no curve, so no stagger is needed.

lessons.title: From Cinders to Rubber
lessons.mainIdea: Tracks changed from dirt and cinders to all-weather rubber surfaces, first used at an Olympics in 1968.
reading: Early tracks were packed dirt or grass. Later, many were covered with *cinders*. Cinders are crushed leftovers from burned coal. Rain turned them soft, and runners' spikes dug deep holes.

In the 1960s, companies made new track surfaces from rubber and plastic. These are called *synthetic* tracks. They drain rain and stay the same in all weather. The 1968 Olympic Games in Mexico City were the first to use one.

Before blocks, sprinters dug small holes in cinders to push from at the start. *Starting blocks* are metal frames that replaced those holes. They came into wide use in the 1930s and 1940s. Today, rule books require blocks for short races at big meets.

words.d: crushed leftovers from burned coal, once used to cover tracks
made by people from materials like rubber and plastic
a metal frame at the start that holds a sprinter's feet

look.title: Two Tracks After Rain
look.text: It rained all night. One track is black cinders. It is soft and full of puddles and deep spike holes. The other track is red rubber. The water has drained away, and the lanes look the same as yesterday.
look.prompt: Which track would give fairer times from one day to the next? Why?

check.q: What are cinders?
check.why: Cinders are crushed leftovers from burned coal.

check.q: Which Olympics first used a synthetic track?
check.why: The 1968 Mexico City Games were the first on a synthetic track.

check.q: What did starting blocks replace?
check.why: Sprinters once dug holes in cinders; blocks replaced them.

lessons.title: The Hand-Held Stopwatch
lessons.mainIdea: Stopwatches let officials write down a race as a time, so meets on different days could be compared.
reading: At first, a race only showed who finished first. A *stopwatch* changed that. It is a watch that starts and stops when a button is pressed. Now each race could leave behind a number.
At early meets, a *timer* stood at the finish with a stopwatch. Several timers often clocked the same runner. Early watches measured to a fifth of a second. Later ones measured to a tenth.
Hand timing has a problem. People press the button a little late or early. So a time from one timer may not match another. Record keepers needed a clock that did not depend on a human thumb.

words.d: a watch that starts and stops by button to measure how long something takes
the official who records a runner's time

look.title: Three Watches, One Runner
look.text: Three timers stand at the finish. One runner crosses the line. The first watch reads 12.2 seconds. The second reads 12.4. The third reads 12.2.
look.prompt: Why might three careful timers get different numbers for one runner?

check.q: What did the stopwatch add to a race?
check.why: A stopwatch turned each race into a time that could be written down.

check.q: What was a problem with hand timing?
choices: People pressed the button a little early or late.
check.why: Human reaction made hand times uneven.

check.q: What does a timer do?
check.why: A timer is the official who records the time.

lessons.title: The Photo Finish
lessons.mainIdea: Cameras and electronic clocks now decide close races and record times to the hundredth of a second.
reading: Sometimes two runners reach the line together. The eye cannot tell who was first. A *photo finish* camera solves this. It points straight along the finish line and takes a picture of the moment runners cross.

Photo-finish cameras spread at big meets in the 1900s. They were joined to electronic clocks. The start signal starts the clock by itself. The camera shows the exact time each runner reaches the line.
This is called *fully automatic timing*. It measures to the hundredth of a second. From 1977, the IAAF accepted world records in short races only if they were timed this way.

words.d: a camera picture taken along the finish line that shows the exact order
timing where the start signal starts the clock and a camera stops it

look.title: A Picture of the Line
look.text: A photo-finish picture shows the finish line as one thin strip. Two runners lean toward it. Beside the picture, a clock reads 11.46 and 11.47 seconds. The judges read the picture, not their memory.
look.prompt: Why might a picture be fairer than a judge's eyes?

check.q: Where does a photo-finish camera point?
check.why: The camera looks along the finish line to catch the exact crossing.

check.q: What starts the clock in fully automatic timing?
check.why: In fully automatic timing, the start signal starts the clock.

check.q: From what year did the IAAF require automatic timing for short-race world records?
check.why: From 1977, those world records needed fully automatic timing.

lessons.title: Illinois Track Since 1893
lessons.mainIdea: IHSA records list state track champions from 1893, before the IHSA was founded in 1900.
reading: The Illinois High School Association, or *IHSA*, was founded in 1900. It runs state tournaments for Illinois high schools. Yet its track records begin earlier. They list state champions from 1893.
Those first meets were held before the IHSA existed. When the IHSA formed, it kept the older results in its records. So Illinois track has one of the longest state title lists in the IHSA's books.

IHSA record books list each year's team champions and event winners. A school in Cairo and a school in Rockford can see the same list. Because both run on 400-meter tracks with the same timing rules, their times can be compared fairly.

words.d: the Illinois High School Association, founded in 1900, which runs state high school tournaments
the team or athlete who wins a state tournament

look.title: Early Illinois Dates
rows: first state track champions in IHSA records

look.prompt: How many years before the IHSA's founding do its track records begin?

check.q: When was the IHSA founded?
check.why: The IHSA was founded in 1900.

check.q: From what year do IHSA records list state track champions?
check.why: IHSA records list track champions from 1893, before the IHSA existed.

check.q: Why can schools in Cairo and Rockford compare their times?
choices: They run the same measured lap with the same timing rules.
They race on the same day in one town.
check.why: Same lap length and timing rules make times comparable.
